intro: A Fourier series builds any repeating pattern out of simple sine and cosine waves, the way a musical chord is built from pure notes. It is the math behind sound, signals and heat flow.

VII.19.01.what: Periodic functions repeat over and over. Sine and cosine waves of different frequencies are orthogonal, meaning they do not overlap in a precise sense.

levels.a: Works with functions that repeat over a fixed length.
levels.b: Shows sines and cosines of different frequencies are orthogonal.
levels.c: Computes integrals of products of sines and cosines.
levels.d: Explains how this lets each wave be picked out from a mix.

VII.19.02.what: Fourier coefficients are the amounts of each wave needed to build a given pattern, like a recipe for a sound.

levels.a: Finds the average level, the constant term.
levels.b: Finds the amount of each cosine wave.
levels.c: Finds the amount of each sine wave.
levels.d: Writes out the full Fourier series.

VII.19.03.what: Building a square wave, which jumps between two levels, from smooth sine waves.

levels.a: Computes the coefficients for a square wave.
levels.b: Sees that only the odd-numbered waves appear.
levels.c: Graphs partial sums getting closer to the square shape.
levels.d: Listens to how adding waves changes the sound.

VII.19.04.what: Building sawtooth and triangle waves from sine and cosine waves, and comparing them.

levels.a: Computes the coefficients for a sawtooth wave.
levels.b: Computes the coefficients for a triangle wave.
levels.c: Compares how fast the amounts of higher waves shrink.
levels.d: Compares how the two waves sound.

VII.19.05.what: A pattern given on half an interval can be extended to use only cosines or only sines, whichever suits the problem.

levels.a: Builds a cosine-only series by mirroring the pattern.
levels.b: Builds a sine-only series by flipping the pattern.
levels.c: Finds half-range series for a pattern given on part of an interval.
levels.d: Chooses which series suits a given problem.

VII.19.06.what: How well a Fourier series matches the original pattern, including a persistent overshoot at sudden jumps.

levels.a: Knows at a jump the series lands halfway between the two levels.
levels.b: Observes the Gibbs overshoot near jumps that never fully goes away.
levels.c: Links smoother patterns to faster-shrinking coefficients.
levels.d: Uses Parseval's identity to add up the energy in all the waves.

VII.19.07.what: Writing Fourier series with complex exponentials, a compact form that combines sines and cosines.

levels.a: Uses complex exponential waves as building blocks.
levels.c: Converts between the complex and sine-cosine forms.
levels.d: Draws a spectrum showing how much of each frequency is present.

VII.19.08.what: The heat equation describes how temperature spreads along a rod. Fourier series solve it by splitting the starting temperature into waves.

levels.a: Understands the heat equation and what it describes.
levels.b: Splits the problem into a time part and a position part.
levels.c: Matches the starting temperature with a sine series.
levels.d: Explains how heat smooths out sharp differences over time.
